changes.from: ### Natural loose parts and a prepared outdoor space
changes.to:
### What the research tells us about children outdoors

Edward O. Wilson, a Harvard biologist, proposed in 1984 that people carry an inborn pull toward other living things (the biophilia hypothesis). It is a hypothesis, and it is still argued over, yet it names something every educator here has seen. A child who walks past a shelf of toys will stop for a lizard on the fence.

Louise Chawla, an environmental psychologist, interviewed adults in Kentucky and Norway who had given their lives to caring for the environment and asked what had shaped them (significant life experiences). In 1999 she reported that the two things named most often were long, free time in wild or half wild places as a child and an adult who showed care for those places alongside them. These were memories looked back on, so they show a link, and a link is all we claim. Her 2007 review of the field found the same pair again and again.

Frances Kuo and Andrea Faber Taylor at the University of Illinois asked whether green places help children attend. In a 2004 national survey, parents of children diagnosed with ADHD reported milder symptoms after time in green outdoor settings than after time indoors or in built outdoor places. In 2009 the same team walked seventeen children, ages seven to twelve, through a park, a downtown and a neighborhood, and the children concentrated best after the park. The samples were older than our children and small, so we say that green settings appear to restore attention and no more. The idea behind their work is Stephen and Rachel Kaplan's 1989 account of attention that recovers in places that hold the eye gently (attention restoration theory).

Richard Louv gathered this research for families in 2005 and named what children lose when they stay inside (nature deficit disorder). The phrase is his, and it is not a diagnosis. It has done its work by getting adults outdoors with children.

### How a child's relationship with a place grows

David Sobel, who taught at Antioch University New England, wrote Beyond Ecophobia in 1996 after noticing that young children taught about rainforests and extinction came away afraid and far away from any forest. He asked educators to let children love the earth before asking them to save it, and he described stages in how children relate to the natural world. Ages four to seven are a time of closeness with animals and small, made places. Ages eight to eleven are for exploring, forts and maps. Only in early adolescence are children ready for the problems of the wider world. All our children sit in or before his first stage, so our outdoors is for closeness, care and wonder, and the hard news of the world waits.

- **Twos and threes.** The same path, the same goat, the same puddle, visited again and again. Place is known through the body and through repetition.
- **Threes and fours.** Small worlds. Homes built for roly polys, names for the chickens, a stump that is always the kitchen. Creatures are treated as someone.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** Routes and maps, a return to the creek to see what changed, questions about where water goes and who lives where, and jobs that keep a place well.

### Why loose parts work

Simon Nicholson, an architect, wrote in 1971 that the amount of invention and discovery in any place rises with the number and kind of things in it that can be moved, combined and changed (the theory of loose parts). A finished playground offers few variables. A pile of sticks, crates, stones and seed pods offers thousands. That is why our outdoor collections stay open ended and why a child's build is left standing for the next day. The Idea bank card Natural materials holds the gathering walks and set-ups, and the Garden, Mud, Creek walks and Oaks and acorns cards carry the places where loose parts gather on their own.

### Natural loose parts and a prepared outdoor space

- [Biophilia, Edward O. Wilson, Harvard University Press, 1984](https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674074422)
- [Life Paths Into Effective Environmental Action, Louise Chawla, The Journal of Environmental Education, 1999](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00958969909598628)
- [A Potential Natural Treatment for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Evidence From a National Study, Frances E. Kuo and Andrea Faber Taylor, American Journal of Public Health, 2004](https://ajph.aphapublications.org/doi/10.2105/AJPH.94.9.1580)
- [Children With Attention Deficits Concentrate Better After Walk in the Park, Andrea Faber Taylor and Frances E. Kuo, Journal of Attention Disorders, 2009](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1087054708323000)
- [Beyond Ecophobia, Reclaiming the Heart in Nature Education, David Sobel, Orion Society, 1996](https://orionmagazine.org/article/beyond-ecophobia/)

### The garden as a learning place, what the research says

School gardens have a long line behind them. Life Lab began in 1979 on a Santa Cruz school site and grew into a garden based science program now based at the University of California, Santa Cruz. Alice Waters began the Edible Schoolyard in 1995 at a Berkeley middle school, where students grow, cook and eat together. Both began from a conviction that a garden teaches, and the research since has been asked to show it.

Dilafruz Williams, who founded the Learning Gardens Laboratory in Portland, and P. Scott Dixon reviewed every study of garden based learning they could find from 1990 to 2010. Their 2013 synthesis of forty eight studies found mostly positive results for science, with smaller and less consistent gains in math and language arts. Many of the studies were small or weakly designed, so the honest claim is that gardens help children learn science and seem to help elsewhere. Williams and Jonathan Brown's 2012 book, Learning Gardens and Sustainability Education, goes further than test results and argues that a garden teaches children to see soil, seasons, water and living things as one connected whole.

David Sobel asked in 1996 that young children be given closeness to living things before they are given the problems of the planet. Louise Chawla found in 1999 that adults who care for the environment most often remembered free time in a wild or half wild place as a child and an adult who tended that place beside them. A planned garden gives both, every season, with an educator who kneels in the bed too.

### How children's understanding of growing develops

Anne Hickling and Susan Gelman at the University of Michigan asked three and four year olds where seeds come from and what they become. In 1995 they reported that by four most children knew a seed comes from a plant of the same kind and grows into that kind of plant, and that plants grow on their own rather than being made by people. Three year olds were less sure. The full circle, from seed to plant to flower to seed again, takes longer to hold in mind, and it is held best by children who have watched it happen.

- **Twos and threes.** Seeds are things to hold, drop and cover. Growth is noticed as change in one plant visited often. Watering is the job.
- **Threes and fours.** Seeds are sorted and named, and children predict what each will become. A plant's needs, water, sun and soil, are talked about and tested.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** Children plan a bed, follow one plant across a season, save its seed and plant it again. Time, sequence and the year as a circle come into reach.

Planning a season ahead lets each class meet the stage its children are in. The Idea bank cards Garden and The orchard through the year hold the set-ups, and Seed to seed follows one plant the whole way round.

### Permaculture as a stance

Bill Mollison and David Holmgren named permaculture in Australia in 1978. Holmgren later set out twelve principles, and the first is to observe and interact. The three ethics beneath them are care of the earth, care of people and a fair share for all. For us permaculture begins as a way of standing in the garden, and the techniques follow. We watch where the sun falls and the water pools before we build. We feed the soil with what the farm already makes. We grow food, flowers and herbs together so that people, pollinators and birds all eat. Children can hold every one of these, and our garden agreements, pick with purpose and leave some for others and be kind to all beings, say them in children's words.

- **The garden as a learning place, How children's understanding of growing develops and Permaculture as a stance.** Williams and Dixon 2013, Williams and Brown 2012, Sobel 1996, Chawla 1999, Hickling and Gelman 1995, Mollison and Holmgren 1978 and Holmgren 2002, with the Idea bank cards Garden, The orchard through the year and Seed to seed, our garden agreements and our age bands.

### What children think a seed is

Jean Piaget asked children in the 1920s what is alive and found that young children often said the sun, the wind or a bicycle were alive because they move. That finding stood for decades. Kayoko Inagaki and Giyoo Hatano, in Japan, looked again and in 2002 reported that by five or six children hold a working biology of their own. They know that living things eat, grow, get sick and get better, and they explain this with a kind of life force that food and water keep up (vitalistic biology). Plants come last. Many five year olds still hesitate to call a plant alive, since it does not move or make a sound, and a garden is where that changes.

Anne Hickling and Susan Gelman found in 1995 that most four year olds know a seed comes from a plant of its own kind and will grow into that kind of plant, while three year olds are less certain. What is inside a seed, and why a tiny seed becomes a tall sunflower, stays a wonder for every age, and we keep it a wonder. The Idea bank card Seeds begins with looking and drawing before any names are offered, and Seed to seed opens a soaked seed to see what is inside.

### Why watering teaches

Inagaki reported in 1990 that kindergarten children who had raised goldfish at home reasoned better about other animals, and about what living things need, than children who had not. Caring for something that can die, and watching what happens when care is given or missed, builds biology faster than being told. Watering is that care in our garden. A child who checks the soil with a finger, carries a full can and sees the soil turn dark where they poured is running a daily test of what plants need.

Dilafruz Williams and P. Scott Dixon's 2013 review of garden based learning found the strongest results in science, and the studies that looked at eating found children more willing to taste a vegetable they had grown. Those studies were mostly with school age children and many were small, so we hold them lightly. Sheri Zidenberg-Cherr's team at the University of California, Davis reported in 2002 that fourth graders with a garden alongside nutrition lessons preferred more vegetables afterward than children with lessons alone. The Idea bank card Watering the garden holds the set-up, and names what carrying a full can gives a body (heavy work, proprioceptive input).

### How sowing and watering grow by age

- **Twos and threes.** Large seeds, beans, peas and sunflowers, pushed into pots with an educator beside them. A small can filled and poured where the child chooses. The job is the whole learning, and a seed that goes in upside down still comes up.
- **Threes and fours.** Seeds sorted by size, with the two lines for the seed tray. Predictions written down and revisited. The finger test, and a tray labeled in the child's own marks. Dividing strawberries, since a baby plant on a runner is a story children can follow.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** Sowing by depth from the seed sizes card, trays kept going through a season, a watering route planned and shared, and a repair watched and helped when the drip line breaks. Children's own tests, such as one tray in sun and one in shade, with the results drawn.

Fine motor control grows along this line too. Pressing one tiny seed into one cell asks for the finger and thumb grip (pincer grasp) that will later hold a pencil, and a two year old who scatters a whole packet is doing the work of their age. The Idea bank card Strawberries carries the ribbon on one flower followed to a berry, which gives the youngest children a single thread to watch.

### Sorting seeds with children

### Why children are drawn to living things

Edward O. Wilson proposed in 1984 that people are born with a pull toward other living things (the biophilia hypothesis). It remains a hypothesis, and some researchers think the pull is learned, yet every educator here has watched a group of children stop a whole walk for one lizard. Louise Chawla's interviews, reported in 1999, found that adults who give their lives to caring for the environment most often remembered two things from childhood, free time in a natural place and an adult who cared for that place beside them. The memories were looked back on, so they show a link and no more. A habitat walk with an educator who crouches too gives both.

### How children's ideas about living things develop

Susan Gelman at the University of Michigan has shown since the early 1990s that preschool children expect living things to have insides that matter and to belong to kinds that hold even when the outside changes (psychological essentialism). A four year old who learns that a caterpillar becomes a butterfly will tell you it is still the same animal. Kayoko Inagaki and Giyoo Hatano reported in 2002 that by five or six children explain eating, growing and getting better in terms of a life force kept up by food and water (vitalistic biology), and that children who care for an animal reason better about all animals. Inagaki showed this in 1990 with children who raised goldfish at home. Plants are the last thing children call alive, and many five year olds still hesitate.

- **Twos and threes.** Creatures are met close up, a snail watched on a leaf, a chicken that comes near. The words are who and where. Gentle hands are learned with an adult's hand beside them.
- **Threes and fours.** Children sort living from not living and are often wrong about plants and about things that move. They give creatures homes, names and feelings, and they ask what a creature eats and where it sleeps.
- **Fours, fives and TK.** Children follow a life cycle from egg to butterfly, map who lives where, and ask what a creature needs and what would happen if it were gone. Food chains, oak to caterpillar to bird, come into reach when the children have seen each link.

The Idea bank cards Bugs and small creatures, Birds and Looking under logs hold the set-ups, and Blooms and pollinators follows the pipevine swallowtail and the ladybug through their stages.

### Native plants, and tools for noticing

Douglas Tallamy, an entomologist at the University of Delaware, counted in 2007 how many kinds of caterpillars feed on each kind of tree and shrub in his region. Native oaks fed more than five hundred, and many ornamental plants from elsewhere fed almost none. Caterpillars are what most songbirds feed their young, so a yard of native plants feeds birds and a yard of imported ones feeds far fewer. His counts were made in the eastern United States, and the pattern holds here. Our valley oaks and coast live oaks are the richest habitat on our site, which is why the Oaks and acorns card asks children to watch for jays and woodpeckers and to map where acorns go. Our pipevine, elderberry, salvias and yarrow were chosen for the same reason.

iNaturalist began in 2008 as a graduate project at the University of California, Berkeley and is now run by the California Academy of Sciences and the National Geographic Society. Every sighting a person adds can be checked by others and used by scientists (citizen science), and our site project keeps our sightings together across years. The app stays on an educator's phone and comes out after children have looked, sketched and said what they think, so its suggestion is one idea to check. Merlin Bird ID, from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, works the same way with sound.

### Plants that feed and shelter
